ddx.step1_summary:
• Chief complaint: Progressive left-sided hearing difficulty and numbness of the left facial/jaw area.
• Symptom details:
  – Onset/duration: ~3 weeks, gradually noticed.
  – Laterality: entirely left-sided.
  – Associated symptoms: intermittent tinnitus (ringing) on the left; occasional dizziness when tinnitus occurs.
  – Negative symptoms: no ear pain, discharge, itching, fever, limb weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria, vision changes.
  – Constant facial numbness currently present.
• Past medical history: Nasal polyps; remote episode labelled “labyrinthitis”.
• Medications: Intermittent intranasal spray for polyps (likely topical steroid); OTC antacid (Rennie).  
• Allergies: Latex.
• Family history: Brother with neurofibromatosis (NF type I/II not specified).
• Social history: 40-year-old female jockey; lives with partner; no pets; no substance use mentioned.
• Vital signs / exam: Not performed (video visit); no objective cranial-nerve or otoscopic findings documented.
• Labs/Imaging: None yet.

V: Ischemic stroke involving brainstem/ACA supply to CN VIII nuclei: unilateral hearing loss/numbness could be vascular, though subacute onset less typical.
Vascular loop compression of CN VIII: arterial loop can cause progressive auditory symptoms.
I: Idiopathic Bell’s palsy (inflammatory facial-nerve neuropathy): could cause facial sensory change and altered sound perception.
Ramsay Hunt (VZV) oticus: facial neuropathy + hearing loss/tinnitus, though usually painful with rash.
Chronic otitis media/mastoiditis: can give conductive loss, but pain/discharge usually present.
N: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma): classically produces unilateral sensorineural loss, tinnitus, imbalance and later facial/trigeminal numbness.
Cerebellopontine-angle meningioma: similar presentation to schwannoma.
Parotid or facial-nerve sheath tumour: facial sensory change + possible hearing involvement.
D: Multiple sclerosis (demyelinating): focal sensory loss, vestibular symptoms possible in 40-yo woman.
Presbycusis/degenerative hearing loss: usually bilateral and gradual; less likely at age 40.
I2: Ototoxic drug–induced hearing loss (e.g., aminoglycosides, cisplatin): no culprit medications reported.
C: Congenital cholesteatoma: unilateral hearing impairment, but rare at 40 and usually gives discharge.
A: Autoimmune inner-ear disease (e.g., Cogan’s, lupus-related): can produce fluctuating unilateral hearing loss and vestibular features.
T: Temporal-bone trauma from falls (possible in jockey): could damage CN VII/VIII producing hearing loss and numbness, though patient denies recent injury.
E: Diabetic mononeuropathy involving facial nerve: no history of diabetes.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Most common cause of progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with tinnitus; can produce facial numbness via trigeminal or facial-nerve involvement. Age and 3-week gradual course fit. Family history of neurofibromatosis increases risk.
supporting_evidence: Progressive unilateral (left) hearing decline over weeks
Brother with neurofibromatosis (NF2 predisposes to schwannomas)
opposing_evidence: No objective neuro exam yet to confirm sensorineural pattern
Relatively short 3-week timeline (tumours usually months); however early presentation possible

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Common cause of acute unilateral facial neurological symptoms; clinician mentioned it. Could rarely present with altered sensation and hyperacusis, but classically causes motor weakness rather than numbness or hearing loss.
opposing_evidence: Facial numbness (sensory) rather than motor weakness/paralysis
Subacute 3-week course rather than acute ≤72 h

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Can cause facial nerve palsy, otalgia, vesicular rash, hearing loss and vertigo. Could explain unilateral symptoms, but pain and rash absent.
opposing_evidence: No ear pain or vesicular rash
Gradual onset over weeks rather than acute

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Young-to-middle-aged woman with focal sensory deficit and intermittent dizziness could represent demyelinating plaque, but isolated cranial nerve VIII/VII involvement without other neuro events is uncommon.
opposing_evidence: Symptoms unilateral and limited; MS usually relapsing/remitting and multifocal
